analysis.one_liner: Caps family health insurance premiums and expands subsidies for people buying coverage on their own.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 37 cosponsors but never received a House vote; it sat in the Ways and Means Committee until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rewrites the Affordable Care Act's premium tax credit so that people buying their own insurance pay a smaller share of their income in premiums — from nothing at the lowest incomes up to a cap of 8.5 percent. It also removes the income ceiling that cuts off the subsidy for families earning above four times the poverty line, so help extends to middle-income households for the first time. It never got a committee vote or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Households buying insurance on the individual marketplace — including people just above the poverty line, whose premiums would drop to zero, and middle-income families currently too well-off to qualify, who would pay at most 8.5 percent of income for coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Slashes the share of income households must pay for benchmark marketplace insurance, ranging from 0 percent at the lowest incomes to a new, lower sliding scale up to 8.5 percent.
Removes the 400-percent-of-poverty income cutoff that currently ends eligibility for premium tax credits, so middle-income families get help too.
Takes effect for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, since the expanded credits have no dedicated revenue source in the bill and add to federal costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill provides no offsetting revenue, so the expanded tax credits would increase the federal deficit, a cost an honest supporter must acknowledge.
The aid flows through private insurers rather than a public plan, which locks in the industry's role and does nothing to lower underlying premiums — it mainly subsidizes what insurers charge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: families buying their own insurance — often self-employed workers, gig workers, and small-business employees without workplace coverage — would see premiums drop sharply, and the middle-income gap in eligibility closes. The main costs are the deficit impact and the choice to route aid through private insurers rather than attack premium prices directly. On balance it is a well-targeted affordability measure, though not one that addresses why premiums are high in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee on January 21, 2021, and no markup, vote, or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lauren Underwood introduced the bill on January 19, 2021 with 14 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day, and to the Subcommittee on Health two days later.
The bill attracted 37 Democratic cosponsors in total but no Republican support.
No further action occurred after the February 4, 2021 introductory remarks; the bill died in committee at the end of the 117th Congress.

Similar premium-credit expansions — extending subsidies above 400 percent of poverty and capping premium contributions at 8.5 percent of income — were enacted later in 2021 through the American Rescue Plan, which passed without this bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and higher-income households gained nothing new from this bill's death, but the same subsidy expansion became law through a different vehicle that year, so marketplace buyers were largely made whole anyway; the cost of Congress's separate-track process was borne by the bill's backers' slower path rather than by consumers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Marketplace buyers, via a later law

for.name: Lauren Underwood
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 37 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican did.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of primary jurisdiction (Chair: Rep. Richard Neal, D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 38 supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the bill also never moved in a chamber controlled by Democrats, so it stalled within the majority rather than against opposition votes.

industries.note: The bill would pour more federal subsidy dollars through private marketplace plans, locking insurers in as the permanent channel for premium assistance while giving them more subsidized customers. Consumers win on affordability in the same stroke, so the industry's interest runs alongside theirs — though the money subsidizes insurer prices rather than lowering them.

The expanded credits have no dedicated funding, so the bill's cost falls on the federal budget. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much weight one puts on affordability versus deficit spending.
